The local quantile treatment effects on the [estimators page](index.qmd) require the instrument to
be valid. The `py-qte` package implements the [Kitagawa 2015](#ref-kitagawa-2015) test for
instrument validity.

For a binary treatment $D$ and a binary instrument $Z$, let $P$ denote the distribution of $(Y, D)$
when the instrument is switched on and $Q$ the distribution when it is switched off. Under the LATE
assumptions of [Imbens & Angrist 1994](#ref-ia-1994), every set $B$ must satisfy

$$
P(B, 1) - Q(B, 1) \ge 0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
Q(B, 0) - P(B, 0) \ge 0,
$$

because both differences are probabilities of a complier's potential outcome falling in $B$. the
`py-qte` package implements Kitagawa's test based on these inequalities. The implementation is
inspired by the original paper and the related R
[`ivcheck`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ivcheck) package; unlike `ivcheck`, it uses
Kitagawa's pooled bootstrap rather than a wild bootstrap.

{{< include _setup-iv.qmd >}}

## The Test Statistic

The test evaluates the inequalities over intervals of the outcome. For each interval and treatment
value it computes the violation of the corresponding inequality; the test statistic is the largest
violation. With `ValidityWeighting.VARIANCE`, each violation is divided by its plug-in standard
error before the maximum is taken, which is the statistic in equation 2.1 of
[Kitagawa 2015](#ref-kitagawa-2015). With `ValidityWeighting.UNWEIGHTED`, the raw violation is used
instead (equation 2.2).

Critical values come from a pooled bootstrap. Replications are drawn from the pooled empirical
distribution of $(Y, D)$, which imposes the null that the two instrument arms have the same
distribution. The p-value is the share of bootstrap statistics at least as large as the observed
one.

```{python}
#| label: lst-validity-config
from qte.bootstrap import BootstrapConfig

VALIDITY_BOOTSTRAP = BootstrapConfig(n_iter=200, seed=42, n_workers=4)
```

## JTPA Assignment

We use the JTPA women sample from the [JTPA Data](index.qmd#jpta-data) section of the estimators
page. Assignment to training is randomized, so the instrument is `assignmt`, the treatment is actual
training, and the outcome is 30-month earnings.

```{python}
#| label: lst-validity-data
from qte.datasets import load_jtpa

jtpa = load_jtpa().filter(pl.col("sex") == 0)
print(f"{jtpa.height} women")
```

## Subdensities

Listing @lst-validity-subdensities shows how to construct the Kitagawa-style joint subdensities
$p(y, d \mid z)$ separately for the two instrument arms and treatment values. These are the
distributions behind the inequalities above: under validity, the instrument-on distribution should
place at least as much mass as the instrument-off distribution on every interval when $d = 1$, and
vice versa when $d = 0$. The figure is a descriptive complement to the formal test, not a test
itself.

```{python}
#| label: lst-validity-subdensities
from qte.iv.descriptives import make_subdensity_plot

subdensities = make_subdensity_plot(
    jtpa,
    "earnings",
    "training",
    "assignmt",
    labels={
        "earnings": "Earnings",
        "training": "Training",
        "assignmt": "Assignment",
    },
    title="JTPA earnings subdensities by assignment and training status",
).configure_legend(orient="bottom")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-validity-subdensities
#| fig-cap: "JTPA earnings subdensities by assignment and training status."
show_chart(subdensities)
```

The figure lines up with the validity inequalities: in the training panel the assigned arm lies
above the unassigned arm, while the reverse holds in the no-training panel.

## Running the Test

`perform_instrument_validity_test` uses `ValidityWeighting.VARIANCE` by default. This standardizes
each interval violation by its plug-in standard error before taking the maximum, which is the
statistic in equation 2.1 of [Kitagawa 2015](#ref-kitagawa-2015). We use this version because it
accounts for the different sampling variability of the interval probabilities. The alternative,
`ValidityWeighting.UNWEIGHTED`, uses the raw positive-part Kolmogorov–Smirnov violation instead
(equation 2.2). The `se_floor` argument bounds the plug-in standard error from below, and
`outcome_grid_size` controls the number of outcome grid points used in the interval search.

```{python}
#| label: lst-validity-test
from qte.iv import ValidityWeighting, perform_instrument_validity_test

with timer("validity"):
    validity_test = perform_instrument_validity_test(
        jtpa,
        "earnings",
        "training",
        "assignmt",
        weighting=ValidityWeighting.VARIANCE,
        bootstrap_config=VALIDITY_BOOTSTRAP,
    )

validity_test.tabulate()
```

The result exposes `statistic`, `p_value`, `verdict` and the most violated interval in `binding`.
`first_stage` is the take-up difference between the two instrument arms; it is negative when the
instrument is coded against the monotonicity direction.
